en: Preface to the Stone Commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* The Buddhist scriptures from the Western Heavens are exceedingly numerous; however, the *Vajracchedikā* alone is the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata’s mind, and it is the supreme treasure of the Chan school.
Having spent many years in contemplation and realization, I have composed this one volume, the *Stone Commentary on the Vajracchedikā*. This is the humble commentary of Yu.
This differs from the common [commentaries]. Each section is divided into four parts: Exegesis, Commentary, Discourse, and Verification.
Following the model of Zhang Juezheng’s *Direct Explanation of the Four Books*, it first analyzes the meaning of each character and subsequently explains them directly in plain language.

The intent is to elucidate the Buddha’s teachings so that students may, through this, achieve realization and personally attain the correct fruition without error. Briefly stated, this is the commentary on this sutra.

There are many interpretations, yet for the most part they are like scratching an itch through a boot—ineffectual. One must attain genuine realization through true inquiry; only then will the mind become clear and the nature radiant.

I shall now speak directly of the source; do not harbor fox-like doubts or discursive thoughts. If you can receive and uphold this with utmost sincerity, opening this scroll will be as clear as seeing the palm of one's hand.
Within this book, the text contains ten articles on the method of reading, ten articles on dispelling delusions, and furthermore, the general...
The essential points distinguish the differences with extreme brevity and clarity. However, each volume of this work consists of one hundred and twenty pages.
I have made a vow to print and distribute ten thousand copies, which I have fulfilled over the course of two years. I regret that my strength is insufficient to provide further copies.
Should there be any faithful patrons, they may purchase paper as they wish; I shall provide the printing blocks for them to print, taking not a single cent from them.

Together we shall assist in this noble undertaking. May all who seek [their goals] have their wishes fulfilled; the merit [thereof] is not inferior to the gift of jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"I only wish that every person may enjoy long life and prosperity"—these were the words of Shao Yong.

Regarding human relations and worldly affairs, whether great or small, refined or vulgar, whatever is beneficial has been recorded by me in plain language and published for the world, comprising both the original and its continuation.

Take the first collection; the second, third, and fourth collections may also be consulted and compiled as convenient, with characters categorized under headings such as filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
However, if this work can be obtained in its entirety, both in its original and supplementary parts, one will likely gain a complete understanding.

Those who can properly embody even a portion of it will surely find their hearts delighted and their spirits at ease, and their blessings and longevity will be long-lasting. Those wishing to seek instruction may go to the Shengping Street Quarter, west of Yangzhou Prefecture.
Inside the gate was the small meditation hall.

In his own preface to the *Stone Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, [the author] stated that while the scriptures of the Western Heaven (India) are exceedingly numerous, the *Vajracchedikā* alone is the root of all sutras. Everything explained within this sutra...

Regarding the esoteric instructions for attaining Buddhahood and becoming a patriarch, since the Tang, Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties, those who have annotated this scripture have numbered no fewer than several hundred families.
Each has exhaustively analyzed the text with their utmost intent, collectively aiming to guide those lost on the path and to awaken future students.
The merit is exceedingly great and the wisdom is exceedingly universal. Regarding the explanations and commentaries of various schools, each has its points of agreement and disagreement;

yet, those who seek a detailed and definitive synthesis remain few and far between. This is truly because they transmit words through words, mostly engaging in mere scholastic research upon the page rather than attaining realization through direct, practical experience. How can one not find this strange? Little do they realize that this sutra...
This is the mind-dharma of the Tathāgata, the fundamental source of the nature of sentient beings. It is the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, yet even this sūtra has no words of explanation.

Because all sentient beings weep over external inducements, they obscure their original spirit; thus, they fall into inverted confusion and wander through the ocean of suffering in saṃsāra—a state most truly pitiable.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has set forth this teaching of true emptiness and signlessness, which does nothing more than to liberate sentient beings.
This commentary unties the bonds and restores one’s original face; it is more than merely a bright lamp in a dark room or the brilliant sun in a gloomy sky.
If you can attain realization, you will immediately realize Bodhi—may you be most sincere indeed!

Now, in remote villages and narrow alleys, wherever there are people of good faith, they all know how to recite the Vajra Sūtra; yet when questioned as to what its principles and meanings are, they remain utterly bewildered.

Yet, they do not understand what this means. Although there are students who have heard the treatises expounded by various masters and have constantly perused the writings composed by different schools, these works are sometimes overly verbose and at other times confused in their meaning.
This merely leaves those who hear or see them utterly bewildered as to whether a point is right or wrong, acceptable or unacceptable, and thus they do not know which way to turn.
Is this not because the Tathāgata’s most subtle and wondrous mind-dharma... [is obscured] by conditions?
That this has not yet been clearly transmitted is deeply lamentable. I, a mere scholar, feel ashamed that my own innate spirit is already half-corrupted by external inducements;
yet, though I remain a layman, I have often practiced the conduct of one who has left the household.
Whenever I have leisure from my Confucian studies, I take the greatest pleasure in reciting this sutra. Thus, it has already been two years since I have devoted my mind to its investigation.
For over ten years, whenever there was a hall where this sutra was being expounded, regardless of its distance, I invariably arrived first.

As for the commentaries on this sutra, whether they were shallow or profound, I invariably examined them all in detail. Although I have heard and seen much, alas, the interpretations differ and are not uniform.
Since this has not yet appeared, how could it inform those of the future? Only the commentary by the Confucian scholar Wang Huailong fully elucidates the subtle and profound essence of the Tathāgata;
moreover, its structure is coherent, concise, precise, and appropriate—neither prolix nor confused.

The merit of this work is indeed great. However, it is regrettable that within the commentary there are passages that do not fully penetrate the meaning of the sūtra, as well as those that contradict the sūtra’s text;
these are like flaws within a jade gem. Undaunted by my own ignorance, I have once again subjected the work to critical revision.

I have excised its partialities and contradictions, supplemented its omissions, and composed a direct interpretation of my own, entitled the *Shizhu* (Stone Commentary). Regarding every single word of the Tathāgata...
These few words are entirely based on my own humble insights, which I have reflected upon and evaluated. It took one year to complete this work, after which I made a vow to carve it for circulation.
I shall print and distribute ten thousand copies to broaden the compassion of the Tathāgata and to fully awaken the wisdom of all sentient beings.
From this day forward, may all virtuous believers who encounter this book seek the Dharma through the sutra and attain awakening through the Dharma, so that the True Teaching [shall flourish].
Thoroughly penetrating and clearly understanding the profound mysteries, one leaves the path of birth and death and ascends the shore of Bodhi.
One extinguishes immeasurable transgressions and attains the most supreme field of merit; realizing the fruits of the human and celestial realms, one shall forever attain happiness.

Only then will one believe that all that is taught in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* constitutes the most supreme secret intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and that what I have said is true and not false. This is my [conviction].
This commentary serves merely to point out the direction of the path for others, so that practitioners may not enter upon rugged or circuitous ways.
It is simply a cause and condition for guidance, should one have the good fortune to meet with the Tathāgata in the future.
May all faithful followers quickly awaken to their original spirit and together return to the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss. Above.
Not to fail the profound intent of the Tathāgata’s instruction, and not to fail my own humble thought of offering even a single point of guidance—
this is truly a source of great joy.
Written on an auspicious day in the second month of the year Renwu, the forty-first year of the Kangxi era, by the lay practitioner Liangjue.

This sutra has been circulated throughout the world; however, many transmitted versions contain errors. Within the realm of the unseen, [the merit] shall endure only through the longevity of one’s kin.
The stone edition by the Southern Tang Dharma Master Daoyong from Qing Temple is taken as the standard. This present work has been entirely revised and corrected according to that stone edition.
All instances of additions, omissions, or errors have been meticulously amended, so that not a single character is in error.
This sutra is divided into thirty-two sections, a tradition handed down from Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty.

However, [the text] is seamless like the sky; to carve and tear it apart would be overly complex. Furthermore, consider the investigation of the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]: one gradually reaches the very crux of the Tathāgata.

Yet, when formerly under Dīpaṃkara, why did he single-handedly inherit the adornment of Buddha-lands? Moreover, the four lines regarding "seeing with form" and "seeking through sound" originally relate to—
The following text flows in a continuous stream, its momentum such that it would be difficult even for a blade to sever like water;

yet, as the chapters and sections follow a systematic order, readers rely upon them for recording and recollection. In this present work, I have merely added fine characters alongside each section to mark their divisions.
One need not read this scripture interspersed with the main text.

In other versions of this sutra, the preliminary sections—including the opening of the scripture, the formal request, and the purification of the mouth—are all later additions by subsequent generations;
these may also be omitted from reading. In this present work, I have deleted them all.
This scripture has been carved into woodblocks many times over the ages; for the most part, it has been entrusted to professional carvers.

Having studied the Song-style characters since my youth, although I have not yet attained mastery, they are roughly sufficient for transcription. Now, this work of mine—every single character and every leaf—has been written by my own hand.
Only after careful collation and verification have I permitted its carving. Readers should rely solely on this edition, which may be trusted as free from error.

Regarding this scripture, it is traditionally said that it was not orally transmitted by eminent monks and must not be read arbitrarily; for fear that errors in phonology and prosody might lead to the incurrence of transgressions.
(I) have personally consulted many monks regarding their pronunciations, each of whom held differing opinions. Now, (I) have further examined and verified them:

where a reading is correct, I have adopted it; where it is incorrect, I have amended it. For each character, I have added direct phonetic transcriptions in small characters as annotations appended to every [character].
Below each section, readers need only rely on these phonetic transcriptions to avoid error.

Although there have been numerous commentaries on this sutra throughout past and present, my current work categorizes each section under four headings: Commentary (註), Discussion (論), Explanation (講), and Verification (證).
This is intended to deconstruct the words and phrases of the main text one by one, all of which are prefaced by the character 【註】.
In general, when discussing the source and flow of the main text, or debating the merits and defects of other commentaries, the character "Lùn" (Discourse) is used as the heading.
As for the character "Jiǎng" (Lecture), everything therein is intended to embody and follow the very tone of the Buddha and Subhūti.
This work expounds the subtle meanings of the original text. If categorized according to the term "Evidence" (證), it consists of four types:

miscellaneous citations of ancient and modern idioms, Confucian texts, monastic sayings, verses, and songs; these are included solely for the purpose of elucidating the subtleties of the original text.

Among these four categories, only the "Exegesis" (講) category contains annotations for every section, while the other three categories—Commentary (註), Evidence (證), and Substantiation (論)—are present throughout.
If a point has already been clarified in the main text or has appeared during the course of the lectures, it is not listed again.
Since the carving of these commentaries on the scriptures, there seems to have been none as shallowly clear and analytically detailed as mine.
Occasionally, there are a few notes that do not follow my revised establishment of the main text; this is because they were chosen for their popular accessibility.
Regarding this scripture, others have either provided separate commentaries or first published the full canonical text and subsequently added detailed annotations following its structural outlines.

Consider, for example, the *Four Books* with Zhu Xi’s commentary; there are those in the world who read only the main text, yet they still read the book that contains the commentary—how could they possibly have perused the main text separately? In my present work, I shall [present] the scriptural text...
The characters are arranged in single columns so that readers may read them by facing the pages; there is no need for separate volumes, nor even for a Sanskrit original.

In other editions of this sutra, only punctuation marks are used, yet it is not easy for those with clear vision to distinguish which parts are the words of the Tathāgata and which are the words of Subhūti. For beginners, such confusion is unavoidable. Therefore, I have composed this work.
All words spoken by the Tathāgata are marked with a circle (○). Words spoken by Subhūti are marked with a black circle (●).
Words compiled by Ānanda are marked with a triangle (△). Words initiating a question-and-answer exchange are marked with connected dots;
through these dots, the sentences become distinct and clear as if held in the palm of one's hand.
Regarding this scripture, other commentaries use only punctuation marks (periods), while others employ circles; however, these are general and lack precision.

In this present work, I shall use a linked circle only for those points concerning the secret instructions on spiritual practice (*kōngfū*). If a phrase is merely subtle, I shall use only a linked period.

For all other instances, I shall follow the standard practice of using black circles at the end of each sentence. Furthermore, any sharp-pointed circles found within the commentary indicate characters from the original text.
This sutra, which I have now composed, though its words may be shallow and mundane, fully expounds the meaning of the Tathāgata’s mind.
Having analyzed and annotated it, I have further transcribed it by my own hand and printed it single-handedly.
I respectfully present this completed work to those of good faith who possess it, exhorting them to always place it upon their desks and to recite the main text with diligence.
One may comprehend and annotate it, or investigate and realize its essential meaning, or expound it for others; otherwise, it is not improper to circulate it widely for the benefit of all.
Most certainly, it must not be placed on high shelves to gather dust and remain sealed away, nor should it be mixed with vernacular novels or theatrical scripts.
Not only would this betray my painstaking efforts, but one would also incur a very grave offense.

Discerning the Differences in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: An Analysis of the Additions, Omissions, and Variations in Words and Phrases. From the absence of a single stroke, it is called *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is called *kṣāntipāramitā*; these are the three phrases concerning ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). If it were not "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñin*), it would be the character "if."
"It is not a first *pāramitā*. The character "is" (*ji*) is a character placed below "for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
The phrase "the foremost Arhat free from desire" and the two characters "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) are all absent from the ancient manuscripts.
Thus, he is named "Anāgāmin" (Non-returner). As for the phrase "Are these many atoms numerous or not?
Subhūti replied, "The four characters [of 'not'] are equal. These are all present in the ancient editions. As in the preceding text, it should read "How does he abide?
rather than, as in the later text, "How should he abide? Since this has been explained in detail, Master Yunqi Shen Bin added special instructions when carving the woodblocks; indeed...
The former question concerns the application of effort; the latter asks who it is that realizes "no-self. The intent of the sutra is distinct in each case.
Furthermore, I have observed that in older editions, the character *jí* (即) was changed to *zé* (則) to avoid the taboo name of the Goryeo king. Generally, *jí* was thus rendered as *zé*.

Later, upon seeing the works of Master Yan of Haiyu, who avoided the taboo name *Wei*, he resolved these various debates by stating that the sense of "uniting two" constitutes *jí*, while the sense of "mutual recognition" constitutes [the other].
Thus, where it is appropriate to use "則" (ze), one may employ it in succession; where it is inappropriate to use "則," one should combine it with "兩" (liang).
One must sigh that the translator again did not alter these words, for by this the adherence to or deviation from the characters "則" and "兩" was finally settled.

Generally speaking, when "則" is used in ordinary application, it merely follows the meaning of the text; by lightly bending [the phrasing] to preserve the overall intent, the "即" (ji) of "非即" (fei ji) further reveals the profound mystery.

Briefly, having completed this single volume for recitation, I have also assisted my fellow students in its examination. I merely wish to extend the spirit of "careful reflection and clear discernment" found within the academic tradition.
As for those who boast noisily of their own ability to distinguish the true from the false, how could I dare to do so?
Dispelling Delusions Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (All Buddhist sūtras should be contemplated in this manner).
Why must one necessarily stay in a quiet chamber?
When people of the world recite the sutras, they mostly seek out quiet rooms; yet they fail to realize that steadfast sincerity resides entirely within the mind and not in the external environment.
If one’s fundamental mind is tranquil, even dwelling amidst the bustle of a marketplace is like being in a remote mountain retreat.
Observe those among our Confucian scholars who excel at reading: they study by the light of a corner-window in a thatched door, or carry their scrolls while tilling the soil. Ultimately...
Success lies therein. Why must it be found in the stillness of a study?
Why necessarily leave the household life?
Leaving the household life is fundamentally for the purpose of escaping such attachments. Yet, I frequently see certain monastics who remain attached to them.
If the mind remains as it was before, though one is called a renunciant, in reality there is no difference between such a person and a layman.
To renounce the world in this manner is actually inferior to remaining a layperson; those who practice the conduct of a renunciant are superior.

Observe that throughout ancient and modern times, there have been many faithful laypeople who attained awakening to Bodhi, such as the Great Master Fu (Bodhidharma’s successor), the Layman Pang, and others.
Having both wives and children as worldly burdens does not hinder one's progress on the Path; it can be seen that this has nothing at all to do with leaving the household life.

Why must one recite sutras at the break of dawn? It is for the sake of attaining utmost sincerity. One must know that if the mind is sincere, even if it were the twelve hours of midday or evening, it would suffice.
There is not a single moment that is not a time for reciting the sutras; to grasp them as soon as the mind reaches them is what constitutes mastery.
Why must one formally request them?
As it says in the sutra: "In whatever place this sutra may exist, all the world—devas, humans, and asuras—"
One should know that wherever this [sūtra] is worthy of being offered to, that place is itself a stūpa; all should pay homage with reverence, circumambulate it, and behold this sūtra.
Whether it be recited or explained, the various devas will arrive of their own accord without being summoned—what need is there to request them?
As for the opening of the sūtra text, such as the mantras for purifying the mouth and so forth: one should read them neither too much nor too little.
Why must one set up images to face the Buddha-image? The intention is to arouse reverence in people; yet they fail to realize that the sutras state:
"All phenomena that possess marks are empty and illusory. If one perceives all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Furthermore, it says: "Those who adorn the Buddha-lands..."
That which is not adornment is what is called adornment. Thus one knows that both adornment and the marks of a Buddha depend entirely upon the sincerity of the mind.
If the mind is not sincere, then even if one is never separated from the sacred image for a single moment, what benefit could there possibly be?
Why must one strike the wooden fish, bells, or chimes? It is simply for their melodic resonance and rhythm; even in their absence, there is no obstruction to the Way.
Why, then, must one recite with haste?

When reciting the sutras, let the text reside in the mouth while the mind contemplates its meaning; one must simply ensure that the characters and phrases are clear and the subtle essence is thoroughly understood.

Even if the recitation is performed in a low, silent voice, it constitutes the Supreme Vehicle. However, if one reads with haste, muddling through for the sake of speed, the words may reach the mouth but not the heart.
Thus, even if one has recited them ten thousand times, if the meaning of the sutra is not understood, it is fundamentally no different from [not having read them at all].
Those who do not read [the scriptures] are the same as those who do. Furthermore, there are those who chant aloud; this merely exhausts their vital energy and is utterly without benefit.

Why must one kneel and recite to contemplate and realize the meaning of the scriptures? Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no time that is unsuitable. Why must one restrict oneself exclusively to [a specific posture]?
Why need one rely on the Sanskrit original?
For the Buddha-dharma fundamentally is not bound to written words. Even these very names of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* are established by force of convention;

how much more so, then, to be constrained by the physical manuscript of the sūtra, whether it be a Sanskrit original? Whether there be gold or pearls within a bag, or merely shards and rubble—it makes no difference.
You speak only of the brocades and silks worn on the outside; I am greatly perplexed by this.
Why must we laypeople remain entirely as such? We cannot avoid the bustle and entanglements of worldly toil; we are not comparable to those who have left the household life and dwell in leisure.
If, while in the midst of reciting a sutra, a pressing matter should suddenly arise, one must wait until this sutra is finished;
would it not be a grave error to do otherwise? If there is indeed urgent business, one need only keep track of the portion reached in the sutra and stop right there.

It would not be improper to wait until the task is finished and then come back to complete it. As for the commentary on this sutra, its profound meanings will not be clarified unless one studies it with meticulous attention.
If one is preoccupied with worldly affairs, how could one possibly read it all at once?

One must understand that when there is a brief respite from mundane matters, one may simply read a single section at any convenient time; by doing so, one will gain the benefit of that section, and as each part is understood, one gains accordingly.

A single portion of this merit—observe how the Sixth Patriarch, on that day, upon hearing only the single phrase from the sutra, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," immediately realized Bodhi.
It is evident that this depends solely on the student's realization through the mind;
how could it be calculated by the number of words and phrases?
General Discourse on the Diamond Sutra:
Since the formation of the human being from the coagulation of the two-fives, all have been endowed with this excellent quality of empty lucidity and non-obscuration;

each, without exception, possesses a single scroll of the True Sutra. Yet, after one is enticed by knowledge and transformed by external objects, the original truth is gradually lost. Although the name remains...

Humans, in truth, are no different from birds and beasts. The *Baopuzi* says: "Human life within the vast canopy of heaven and earth proceeds from youth toward maturity, and from maturity toward old age;
with every step taken, one moves closer to death, like leading an ox or a sheep to the slaughterhouse."
With every step forward, one draws closer to death; how can one not stand in awe?

Therefore, our Buddha, out of necessity, employed provisional and skillful means to guide and lead those who are deluded. What is "life and nature"? What is "cultivation"? He forcefully gave them names and called them "Sūtras.
If there were a heroic man of noble character who realized the fundamental essence for himself, how could he rely upon verbal explanations?
Then the true scripture is revealed. This true scripture is inherently possessed by every person; it is lacking in none.

It is not realized because of being a sage, nor is it diminished by being an ordinary person. It does not employ written words, nor does it require commentary. There is no need for carving, printing, recitation, or study.
One must know it; one knows it immediately. It is not difficult at all. If one does not know it, all efforts will be in vain, and in the end, nothing will be known.

As long as one possesses this true scripture, all other scriptures are of no use. Though they may be arranged with brocade rollers and ivory bookpins, they serve merely as objects for veneration. If this true scripture is not known, there is no choice but to bring it forth.
One circles the texts and exhaustively investigates their profound depths, deliberating upon them day and night.

When, after a long period of diligent effort, one suddenly attains a sudden and thorough penetration, one finally becomes a person of supreme learning, non-action, and great joy. This is the teaching that "there is no dharma to be spoken."
These words are not false.
Regarding the ten rules for reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
the phrases and sentences of the *Vajracchedikā* are repetitive, yet each possesses its own principle; they are profound and subtle, unlike the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* or the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
Yan. This may be compared to that which is detailed, clear, and easy to understand. Readers must examine it with careful attention before they can perceive its subtle profundity.

In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the four bodhisattvas—Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and Akṣayamati—are none other than the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
they are the bodhisattvas within our own bodies. Readers must first possess such states of mind before they can enter the Great [Vehicle].
By practicing the Way, one awakens to the meaning of the Vajra.
Although there are many men and women who recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, those who attain realization of the Vajra are very few.

This is entirely because they rely on mere verbal recitation and do not know how to contemplate and awaken to the wondrous Dharma. Those who read it must sit in stillness and observe the mind; when the mind is free from...
Settle your mind, and then take up this commentary to contemplate it; in this way, you may hope for progress.
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there is no part of the first half that is not expounded here, nor is there any part of the latter half that is not fully encompassed.
From the seventeenth section, it further explains the passage on "how one should abide," gathering the entire purport without remainder. Hereafter—
What was previously detailed is here abbreviated; what was previously abbreviated is here detailed. Each section follows upon the next, each possessing its own subtle meaning.
Although the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* contains many words, they all expound the wondrous principle of true emptiness and formlessness in order to transform and deliver sentient beings.
This requires that sentient beings be able to abide securely and subdue their minds, so as not to give rise to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
Once one has emerged into the stage of *nirvāṇa*, the teaching on giving (*dāna*) serves merely to make the practice easy to enter;
it is not fundamentally emphasized. Regarding the primary meaning of the sutra, all matters are exhausted within the principle of "abiding" (*sthiti*).
From the fifth division onward, much of the discourse merely reiterates and clarifies the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), fearing that people...
First, if one clings to having marks (sanimitta), one will be unable to abide in and subdue [the mind].
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha taught non-mark (animitta); this merely removes deluded thoughts, but does not remove the principle of Heaven (tianli).

If one were to eliminate the principle of Heaven as well, one would inevitably become a walking corpse or a wandering piece of flesh, living in vain within this world. Therefore, it is said in the fourteenth section:
The three characters for "the reality of birth" (sheng shi xiang) also concern the fear that people might drift toward aridity and withered emptiness.
If our Confucian scholars do not investigate this in detail, but instead claim that the Buddhists advocate for vacuity and extinction, is this not a grave transgression?
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, when the Buddha speaks of "greatness," he refers to Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains;
when he speaks of "muchness," he refers to that which is equal to the sands of the Ganges River; and when he speaks of "long duration," he refers to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
These are indeed based on the principle of inexhaustible numbers—extremely great, extremely many, and extremely long. It is neither an exaggeration by the Tathāgata, nor...
The Tathāgata delights in using such expressions to startle the mundane world; readers should seek their underlying principle. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* repeatedly speaks of giving;
while giving with signs (*sanimitta-dāna*) certainly does not cease to be a form of cultivation, it cannot be discussed as the wondrous meaning of the *Vajra*.
If there is a person of good faith who regards the supreme treasure within their own body as neither arising nor ceasing—
Riding upon clouds of fragrant flowers, one enters boundless realms and gives rise to platforms of radiant light to make offerings to the ten directions;
this is the merit of perceiving one's nature, which far surpasses these [other deeds].

In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, within the section "Arising in Accordance with the Dharma," it is stated that even if one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, it would not equal the merit of upholding this sūtra.

In the section "The Superiority of Unconditioned Merit," it is further noted that filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures—even more than the aforementioned trichiliocosm—still does not equal the merit of upholding this sūtra. thus there shall be such true knowledge, such true vision, and furthermore, such faith, acceptance, understanding, and realization."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is entirely present within my own innate, true nature.

As for all external phenomena that possess form and trace—anything capable of obstructing my true mind—it simply does not arise within that mind. Now, as for what I have called "dharmalakṣaṇa" (the characteristics of phenomena):
although these things appear to be external, they are compliant and empty; fundamentally they do not reside within me, and thus they are not the Dharma.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to that which can be pointed out as having a physical form or trace; these are merely provisional names for "dharma-characteristics.
Since dharma-characteristics are ultimately non-existent, there can certainly be no views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
These are precisely what the true mind of bodhi should know, see, believe, and understand. Those who have resolved to attain bodhi—how can they fail to examine this?
Chapter Thirty-Two: On the Manifestation of Transformation Not Being Real.
Subhūti, if there were someone who took seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offered them as a gift;
and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and holds this sutra, even...
If one receives, maintains, reads, recites, and explains even as little as four lines of verse from this sutra to others, their merit shall surpass that of the former.
[Note: "Immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds" means not merely those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"One who gives rise to the Bodhisattva mind" refers to one who generates the vast resolve to deliver all sentient beings; this is precisely the *bodhicitta*.

[Commentary] The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "If there were someone who filled immeasurable and infinite worlds with the seven treasures and bestowed them as gifts upon others, this would indeed constitute worldly merit.

However, if there are men or women who give rise to the Bodhisattva’s mind of universal salvation and do not merely uphold these verses of this sutra, but instead realize their own nature and further expound them [to others], [their merit shall be far greater]."
To teach others to see their own nature so that both self and others achieve perfection—this is supramundane merit, the enjoyment of which is inexhaustible. How could this not surpass that?
[Commentary] Master Chengfanchangruo explained that this sutra takes the deconstruction of marks as its primary tenet and the realization of emptiness as its meaning.
To practice giving while deluded regarding the nature of reality does not lead to the realization of truth; only by being able to recognize the fourfold gate of nirvana can one do so.
To expound the Dharma-body, which is suchness and immovable, and to contemplate conditioned phenomena as being identical to dreams and illusions—
if one acts with this vision to teach and transform sentient beings, it is superior to the merit gained from giving gifts of the seven treasures.
"How does one expound the teaching for others? Without grasping at signs; suchness is immovable.
[Commentary] These two phrases, "without grasping at signs," encompass the essential purport of the entire sutra.
The very spirit and life-vein of the Buddha reside herein. One should realize this through the mind.
[Commentary] The Buddha asks himself: "How should one expound these four lines of verse to others?
He then answers himself: "Do not grasp at appearances; remain as suchness, unmoving.

This is because my true nature is the wondrous mind of supreme Bodhi and the actual principle of Nirvana without remainder. Here, both person and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished. Sentiment...
Wisdom and [its object] are both forgotten; naturally, there are no traces to be sought, nor are there sounds or forms to be seen.
One does not cling to self, person, sentient being, or life-span. One does not dwell in form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects (*dharmas*).
Originally empty and true, what characteristic could there be to grasp? One sees only suchness (*tathatā*), which is spontaneously so, as one.

He manifests spiritual powers throughout the Dharma-realm, yet his concentration is inherently true. Myriad transformations are wondrously beyond fixed direction, yet his essence is eternally quiescent.
Though he brings sentient beings to extinction, there is no one who exists; though he practices giving and adornment, he is without a mind.
His deportment is merely tranquil, and his cognition and vision are merely non-arising. He abides eternally throughout the entirety of the void-like world, yet never...
This is movement. These are the true four lines by which one may expound. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and also like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.

[Note] Dreaming involves emerging from a state of no-mind; illusion involves being formed with intention. Awakening from a dream is entering into illusion; the formation of illusion is the binding of doubt and dreaming.
All arise from inversion. A bubble is formed from water; as the water subsides, the bubble vanishes. A shadow is produced by the reflection of a form; as the form ceases, the shadow perishes.
Both are empty and lack substantiality. Dew is dried by the sun; lightning disperses when the rain clears. These, moreover, arise and vanish in an instant.
"Extinction. Within these six characters, the responses of human affairs, the stability of mountains and rivers, and the transformations of heaven and earth are all fully explained.
These four phrases completely encompass the essential purport of the scriptures; they are precisely the Tathāgata’s point of true and earnest *nirvāṇa*.
They represent the wondrous wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness, the contemplation of the provisional, and the contemplation of the middle.
[The Master] further enlightened him, saying: "As for what I call 'suchness' (tathatā) and 'immovability,' why is this so?
It is because the true emptiness is signless and fundamentally such as it is. All worthies and sages have personally realized it through the dharma of non-action (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
If there were any affairs of worldly activity, they would all be empty, false, and unreal, like a dream."

One should contemplate these six points as being unreal: like a magical illusion, like a bubble on water, like a flickering shadow, like morning dew that quickly dries, and like a flash of lightning that swiftly vanishes.
By observing them in this way, one can see that all worldly phenomena and conditioned things (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they all arise and subsequently perish.
It is not that they truly exist. It is only my nature of suchness, which is immovable; profound as the great void, it transcends ten thousand kalpas and remains forever.
To expound this for others—how could its merit and virtue ever come to an end?
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras— hearing what the Buddha had said, were filled with great joy.
Believe, accept, and practice [this]. (The pronunciation of "bi" is like that of "bi").

[Commentary: Since the Buddha had repeatedly and extensively expounded the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā and completed his preaching of the sutra, the elder named Subhūti—who had first requested the teaching, attained sudden enlightenment into the true emptiness, and had already received the seal of the mind—[was present] at that time.
Among those who heard the Dharma at that assembly, there were bhikṣus whom they called "monks"; there were bhikṣuṇīs whom they called "nuns" (shigū);
there were laymen whom they called *upāsakas*; and there were female practitioners of the Way whom they called *upāsikās*.
This included all people of the world, as well as the devas of the heavens and the asuras.
The deities of Mount Lu, having heard this sutra spoken by the Buddha, each declared that they had realized the nature of the mind beneath them.
Without alarm, without terror, and without fear, they were all filled with great joy. Fortunate to have encountered the True Dharma so rarely, they delighted in having personally met it this day.
There was none who did not believe and accept his words, internalizing them in their hearts; there was none who did not practice his teachings and propagate them to others.
Although it has been billions of kalpas since [this was attained], one will forever realize the indestructible vajra-body. The Buddha’s compassion is ultimate;
those who behold this sutra shall repay the Buddha’s kindness.
【Testimony】 Master Chuan’s Verse says: Hungry, one finds food; thirsty, one finds drink. Ill, one finds recovery; hot, one finds coolness.
A poor man encounters treasure; an infant sees its mother. A drifting boat reaches the shore; a solitary traveler returns home. In drought, one meets sweet rain.
The land possesses loyal and virtuous men; the four barbarian tribes fold their hands in submission, and all within the eight directions come to surrender. Every single thing is thus;
every object fully manifests [the truth]. From the sages and ordinary beings of past and present, to the hells and heavens, to the east, west, south, and north—there is no need for deliberation.
All beings throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust and grains of sand have entirely entered the Great Diamond Path.
